For 10 points, give this quoted question, deployed online as an ironic reaction caption, that a Ugandan talk-show host actually posed to a real LGBT activist on air.
answer: Why are you gay? [or Why are you gae]

question: An anonymous user started this concept on 4chan's paranormal board on 12 May 2019, inviting others to post unsettling photos that simply felt "off." The original post paired that invitation with an image of an empty, yellow-carpeted hallway, captioned with the claim that "noclipping" out of bounds in real life could strand a person inside an endless maze of similar rooms. A dedicated wiki cataloguing further lore and monster entries launched roughly two months later, in June 2019, cementing the concept as one of the defining examples of the liminal-space aesthetic. For 10 points, name this creepypasta setting, an unsettling maze of empty office-like rooms accessible by glitching out of reality.

The earliest known use of this deliberate misspelling appeared in a Reddit post on 11 December 2020, though it didn't catch on until over a month later. On 16 January 2021, Redditor Lewdvik posted an edited panel from the webcomic StoneToss, replacing its original dialogue with this misspelled phrase and inserting a crudely drawn crewmate, specifically as a way to mock and deface that neo-Nazi-associated comic. The edit went viral, and the template of replacing comic dialogue and captions with this word alongside a badly drawn crewmate spread rapidly afterward. For 10 points, give this intentionally misspelled internet nickname for the video game depicted by that crudely drawn crewmate.

Literally combining words for a part of the body and a piece of fabric, this Jamaican Patois term's original meaning refers to a menstrual cloth, giving it strong taboo weight in its home culture. Divorced from that context, English-speaking TikTok users around 2019 began captioning surprising videos and images with the single word as a stand-in for 'can you believe this,' turning it into an all-purpose exclamation of shock. Commentators have criticized its casual meme use by people unfamiliar with the term's original, more vulgar meaning as culturally insensitive. For 10 points, give this Jamaican Patois exclamation of shock or dismay that became a viral TikTok caption meme.

This line comes from a Nigerian Nollywood film called Pretty Liars, in which a man chases down a woman fleeing his car before confronting her with the titular question. Vine user Sam Iglesia helped popularize the clip in mid-2016, racking up over a million loops on the now-defunct app. The phrase reached a new audience in 2018, when YouTuber Syrmor's video of gangs of Ugandan Knuckles characters swarming other players in VRChat while chanting it went viral. For 10 points, give this line, shouted by a man chasing a woman in a Nollywood film clip, later adopted as a taunting chant by Ugandan Knuckles mobs.
answer: Why are you running [or Why are you running?]

question: One panel of this two-image format captures Taylor Armstrong mid-meltdown during a season two episode of The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills that first aired in December 2011. The other shows a white feline, photographed by owner Miranda Stillabower after he hopped into an empty dinner chair left with a plate of salad still in front of it. Twitter user MISSINGEGIRL first paired the two images on May 1st, 2019, and the combination exploded into one of the year's biggest memes, later winning Meme of the Year at the Shorty Awards. For 10 points, name this meme pairing a screaming reality TV star with a confused-looking feline seated at a dinner table.
answer: Woman Yelling at a Cat [or Woman Yelling at Cat; or Smudge the Cat]

question: A remix of this instrumental track by producer g3ox_em has soundtracked more than 742,000 separate TikTok videos, part of a sprawling family of remixes that also includes slowed-and-reverb, bass-boosted and orchestral Two Steps From Hell-style renditions. g3ox_em has also released mashups combining it with other viral tracks, including one pairing it with the German song "Gut Genug." Untethered from its original meme entirely, editors now drop it under any clip meant to convey an unstoppable, triumphant transformation. For 10 points, give the title of this bombastic instrumental track, named for and closely associated with an internet meme depicting an idealized, chiseled image of masculinity.
answer: GigaChad Theme [or GigaChad Theme (Phonk House Version); prompt on Gigachad]

question: Real name Eric Knudsen submitted the earliest images of this figure to a June 2009 Something Awful forum contest challenging users to Photoshop "paranormal images," adding a tall, faceless figure to ordinary black-and-white photos of groups of children alongside fabricated witness testimony about their disappearances. Knudsen, posting under the pseudonym Victor Surge, copyrighted the character's name in January 2010. A 2012 indie horror game about this figure, along with the YouTube found-footage series Marble Hornets, helped cement him as a horror-gaming icon, while a widely covered 2014 stabbing case carried out by two children hoping to "prove the skeptics wrong" brought the character infamy far beyond internet horror circles. For 10 points, name this tall, faceless creepypasta figure in a black suit.

This prank traces its name to an earlier 4chan bait-and-switch meme called duckrolling, in which a misleading link led instead to an image of a duck on wheels. On 15 May 2007, 4chan user Shawn Cotter uploaded a music video to YouTube and linked it in place of a promised trailer for the video game Grand Theft Auto IV. 4chan founder Christopher "moot" Poole later credited the prank, in a 2010 TED Talk, with single-handedly reviving the music video's singer as a pop-culture touchstone nearly two decades after his 1980s heyday. For 10 points, name this bait-and-switch prank, in which an unsuspecting victim clicks a link expecting one thing and instead gets the music video for "Never Gonna Give You Up."

This reaction image comes from the tenth episode of the original Pokemon anime, "Bulbasaur and the Hidden Village," first aired in June 1997, during a scene where a wild Bulbasaur blows sleep powder back at Ash's Butterfree. The exaggerated, wide-eyed, gaping-mouth expression belongs to a background character who wasn't the focus of the shot, a result of the animators not fully polishing a minor reaction shot. The image sat unused as a meme for over two decades until Tumblr user Angela paired it with a joke about predictable outcomes on 26 September 2018, and it became one of the internet's most versatile reaction images within a week. For 10 points, name this exaggerated reaction meme starring Ash Ketchum's iconic yellow rodent companion.

Canadian artist Trevor Henderson, then posting under the handle Slimyswampghost, introduced this character in an August 2018 Twitter post describing a woman who spotted it standing in a cemetery while driving past. Standing roughly forty feet tall, its body is depicted as rusted metal and mummified skin, with two functioning emergency loudspeakers in place of a face, wired to its neck. Though not technically part of the SCP Foundation's canon, it is closely associated with that wider genre of collaborative online horror fiction. For 10 points, name this towering monster with emergency loudspeakers where a face should be, created by Trevor Henderson.

Content creator Jools Lebron posted the original video coining this catchphrase on 5 August 2024, jokingly describing her own makeup routine and airplane deboarding etiquette using the term. The full phrase, paired with a related term for careful, intentional self-presentation, quickly racked up over 45 million views and drew both celebrity and corporate brands eager to cash in on the trend, widely read as a gentle mockery of aesthetic-obsessed "clean girl" influencer culture. Dictionary.com later crowned a shortened form of this catchphrase's key adjective its 2024 Word of the Year. For 10 points, give this two-word viral catchphrase, popularized by Jools Lebron, describing modest, reserved self-presentation.

Beijing-based actor and director Zhang Aiqin, nicknamed "Brother Egg" online for his bald, oval-shaped head, filmed himself singing this line while walking alone through a heavily snow-covered park in a January 2020 video posted to the platform Kuaishou. The line comes from Taiwanese singer Fei Yu-ching's 1983 song "Yi Jian Mei," actually a melancholic love song that uses winter plum blossoms as a metaphor for love enduring hardship, though the meme strips away that context entirely. After spreading through Instagram edits in March 2020, the sound reached international TikTok audiences by May, propelling the decades-old song to the top of Spotify's Viral 50 charts in several countries. For 10 points, give this Mandarin lyric, translating to "snowflakes are fluttering, the north wind is howling," now used as an ironic meme caption for cold or bleak situations.
answer: Xue Hua Piao Piao [or Xue Hua Piao Piao Bei Feng Xiao Xiao; or 雪花飘飘]

question: This dismissive retort is delivered by an off-screen adult in the same six-second Vine responsible for the "9 + 10 = 21" meme, immediately after the boy in the video gives his confidently incorrect answer. Before Vine's shutdown, the clip amassed more than 30 million loops and 700,000 likes. Distinct from the boy's wrong numerical answer itself, this specific put-down became its own separate stock reaction line, often captioned under clips of someone making an obviously foolish mistake. For 10 points, give this two-word insult, snapped at a boy after he confidently answered a simple addition problem incorrectly in a famous 2013 Vine.

YouTuber Drew Gooden posted the Vine behind this quote on 20 March 2016, misreading a construction sign's message as a question rather than a statement. The six-second clip gathered over 127,000 revines and 10 million loops, and has followed Gooden for years afterward as an inescapable catchphrase, one he eventually leaned into by selling merchandise built around it. For 10 points, give this deliberately obtuse response to a warning sign, misinterpreting a warning about construction as an inquiry.
answer: Road work ahead? Yeah, I sure hope it does [or Road work ahead; prompt on partial answer]

question: British teenager Tish Simmonds posted the Vine behind this sing-song quote on 21 July 2014, filming themselves sitting in the driver's seat before their mother, off-camera, responds by telling them to get out of the vehicle. Within two weeks the clip had gathered more than 165,000 likes, and a house remix posted to YouTube by SalemKhazili helped push the audio further into music-remix circles. Even after Vine's 2017 shutdown, the quote's closing onomatopoeia remained a stock caption British internet users still drop into unrelated driving videos. For 10 points, give this sing-song Vine quote, delivered in a strong Yorkshire accent, describing a joyride that never actually leaves the driveway.
answer: I'm in my mum's car, broom broom [or I'm in me mum's car, broom broom; prompt on partial answer]

question: This sung line comes from an episode of Parks and Recreation, performed by the sibling duo Jean-Ralphio and Mona-Lisa Saperstein as they tiptoe through their father's office building trying to win back jobs they'd just been fired from. The irony driving the clip's humor is that their exaggerated tiptoeing and comically wide-eyed glancing make them by far the most conspicuous people in the building. Years after the show aired, the clip became an organic TikTok sensation, with users setting the audio over clips of animals or people caught behaving conspicuously despite their best efforts to appear casual. For 10 points, give this ironic, twice-repeated instruction, sung while doing the exact opposite of following it.
answer: Don't be suspicious, don't be suspicious [or Don't be suspicious; prompt on partial answer]

question: Swedish influencer Saskia Cort first encouraged followers to ask their male partners this question in 2023, and the prompt resurfaced that August when history enthusiast Gaius Flavius, also based in Sweden, posted the same idea to Instagram, from which it exploded onto TikTok in September. Videos showing women asking the men in their lives how often they think about this topic, and the surprisingly high frequency of the answers, drew over 1.6 billion combined views. The trend has since evolved into a general catchphrase for anything someone can't stop thinking about, whatever the actual subject. For 10 points, give this ancient Mediterranean civilization, subject of a 2023 TikTok trend about male preoccupation with history.

A 57-year-old Venetian woman named Monica, part of a decades-old volunteer group patrolling for thieves, is the voice behind this shouted Italian warning, captured on video by the TikTok account @cittadininondistratti2. After that original account was suspended in June 2023, a replacement quickly regained an even larger following. Though originally meant literally, to warn tourists near Venice's canals and vaporetto stops, the audio clip has since been layered over completely unrelated videos of people and animals caught in humorously compromising situations. For 10 points, give this shouted Italian exclamation, warning that a thief is nearby.

Alleged to have originated on 4chan's weapons board around 2010, this viral text boasts of having 'over 300 confirmed kills' and being 'trained in gorilla warfare,' as an anonymous internet tough guy exaggerates his credentials while threatening someone who has insulted him online. Its absurd, hyper-aggressive tone made it one of the most copied and parodied blocks of text on the internet, spawning translated, animal-themed, and corporate-friendly remixes for over a decade. It opens with a string of profanity before pivoting into the exaggerated military resume. For 10 points, give the opening line of this famous viral text, a profanity-laden threat directed at someone who has insulted a self-proclaimed military commando.
answer: What the fuck did you just fucking say about me, you little shit? [or What the fuck did you just fucking say about me, you little bitch?; or Navy Seal Copypasta; prompt on partial answer]

question: This shock-comedy persona's creator, George Miller, retired the character in December 2017, citing health concerns, before reinventing himself as the R&B and hip-hop musician Joji. Posting first through his channel DizastaMusic before moving to a dedicated channel in 2014, Miller ran the character's show from August 2011 to September 2017, mixing absurdist, deliberately offensive sketches with spinoff characters like Pink Guy and Salamander Man. A February 2012 video from this channel is credited with kicking off the viral 'Harlem Shake' dance meme the following year. For 10 points, give the stage name of this shock-comedy YouTube character created by George Miller.

This YouTuber's 'Content Cop' series has targeted numerous other creators for hypocrisy or bad behavior, including an April 2025 installment aimed at podcaster Ethan Klein amid an ongoing feud. He also hosts 'Kickstarter Crap,' a series mocking poorly conceived crowdfunding campaigns that grew out of a March 2013 video originally titled 'Gaming News Crap.' In 2021 he founded Creator Clash, a boxing event pitting online creators against each other, and he is married to fellow creator Anisa Jomha. For 10 points, name this YouTuber known for his snarky commentary series and triple-B stage name.

The host of this educational channel originally intended to name his channel 'Video Game Nation' at a sponsor's request, but disliked it and instead generated a random, pronounceable name using a fake-domain generator website. Early videos focused on gaming before his philosophical and scientific 'DOT' series proved so popular that it reshaped the channel's entire focus, eventually leading to spinoff channels fronted by hosts Kevin and Jake. Nearly every video from the main channel opens with this exact catchphrase before diving into a rabbit hole of a question like 'what if everyone on Earth jumped at once?' For 10 points, give this catchphrase, an educational YouTuber's self-introduction, featuring the host's first name.
answer: Hey, Vsauce. Michael here. [or Vsauce Michael here; prompt on partial answer]

question: Since a June 2013 Perth television interview, in which the creator's identity was kept hidden per his request, almost nothing has been confirmed about the person behind this channel beyond his home country. Its videos mimic the structure of ordinary tutorial content before escalating into absurd, destructive chaos involving household objects and food. YouTube suspended the channel outright on two occasions, in 2014 and again in late 2015, over presumed violations of its policy on misleading content. A long-anticipated face-reveal video became one of the platform's most notorious trolls, when several well-known YouTubers each stepped forward claiming to be the anonymous creator. For 10 points, name this anonymous Australian YouTube channel, launched in December 2011, known for its titular parody tutorials that spiral into destructive absurdity.

This genre's name is a portmanteau of Korean words for 'eating' and 'broadcast,' and it grew out of marathon livestreams on the platform AfreecaTV in the early 2010s, where hosts called BJs, or broadcast jockeys, kept viewers engaged for hours at a stretch. Hosts converse with their audience while working through a table piled with indulgent food, creating a simulated sense of dining together that researchers link to combating isolation in a hyper-online era. In 2021, the Oxford English Dictionary added the term, alongside a wave of other Korean loanwords, acknowledging its spread well beyond South Korea to YouTube and Twitch worldwide. For 10 points, give this Korean term for a video genre centered on watching someone eat, often huge quantities of food, on livestream.

The video behind this exclamation shows a disc golf throw sailing wildly off course, nowhere near its intended basket, prompting an off-screen voice to erupt with this line at the thrower. Originally circulated as a Vine, the clip has since become a stock reaction clip, dubbed over unrelated footage of blunders, mishaps and unforced errors of all kinds. Its target's first name has become a punchline in its own right, synonymous with baffling incompetence. For 10 points, give this exasperated exclamation, directed at the disc golfer, that became a viral reaction meme for any obviously bad decision.
answer: What the fuck, Richard?! [or What the heck, Richard?; prompt on partial answer]

question: This six-second Vine clip's exact origin and original speaker remain largely undocumented, but the audio has taken on a life of its own as one of the platform's most remixed and dubbed-over meme sounds. Its final word is stretched out for comedic emphasis, distinguishing it from countless other declaration-of-devotion soundbites online. Creators frequently overlay the audio onto unrelated footage, using its earnest, over-the-top declaration for ironic contrast against mundane or chaotic images. For 10 points, give this repeated, over-the-top Vine-era declaration of undying devotion, memorable for how its last word is drawn out into several syllables.
answer: I love you bitch, I ain't never gonna stop loving you, biiiiitch [prompt on partial answer]

question: Originating from an August 2023 tweet by user BronGotGame, this glowing, over-the-top paragraph of praise typically opens with the words 'Boy oh boy, where do I even begin,' building through increasingly hyperbolic compliments before an anticlimactic final reveal of its subject. The format exploded into mass use in early 2024 alongside other memes about the same subject, like 'You Are My Sunshine' edits and jokes about his nicknames, before trending heavily on TikTok that March. Users now swap in any name, mundane or absurd, for comedic effect, though the format's namesake remains the NBA superstar originally being 'glazed.' For 10 points, give this basketball star's name, the punchline completing the viral 'glazing copypasta' format.

This short Vine-era clip is frequently recirculated in reaction videos and remix edits, and has become closely associated with YouTuber iDubbbz, who has shared or referenced it among his own content. The line is delivered as a flat, deadpan non-sequitur, often dubbed over unrelated footage of someone taking a fall or otherwise showing sudden physical frailty for comedic incongruity. Precise details of its original creator and context have been lost to internet history, as is common for short-form Vine-era audio memes. For 10 points, give this deadpan medical complaint about weakened, brittle bones, a stock punchline for comedic falls online.

TikToker Alfonso Pinpon kicked off this trend on February 25th, 2024, by approaching strangers in a mall and posing a language-choice question, then declaring that whoever moved first would be considered gay. Countless imitators filmed their own version of the freeze-tag-style prank, asking their target the same either-or question before delivering that same stakes-raising punchline. One particular edit, posted by TikToker dr1nkz7 that May, racked up over 39 million plays within a week. For 10 points, give this three-word either-or question that opens a viral TikTok prank format, asking a stranger which of two languages to use before a freeze-game challenge.
answer: English or Spanish [or Do you speak English or Spanish?]

question: This phrase emerged from online gaming communities as a rival chant after Twitch streamer AngryPug provoked players on an H1Z1 server in a July 2015 clip by praising Taiwan instead. A separate, widely circulated audio clip of someone enthusiastically declaring the phrase, often paired with a similar line about Korea, became a go-to sound bite for reaction videos and ironic-praise edits, frequently associated with streamer iShowSpeed's content. Both versions play on exaggerated national pride as a punchline, whether provoking rival gamers or mockingly hyping up an unrelated topic. For 10 points, give this enthusiastic three-word declaration of national pride, a viral meme phrase used both to provoke online gamers and ironically praise something.

Though widely treated as a standalone clip, this video was actually a trailer for a full-length Brazilian fetish film titled 'Hungry Bitches,' produced by MFX Media and released in 2007. Its extreme scatological content shocked viewers so badly that filming other people's horrified reactions to it became a viral phenomenon in its own right, helping establish the 'reaction video' as its own YouTube genre practically overnight. Its cultural reach extended well beyond shock sites, drawing references on network shows including The Office and a parody on Family Guy. For 10 points, give the title of this infamous, graphic 2007 internet video, whose four-word title counts the performers and their shared vessel.

This pejorative pairs a verb meaning to impress spectacularly, popularized within 1970s and 80s Black and Latino LGBTQ+ ballroom culture as a metaphor for "killing it" with style, and a noun for a woman of power and status. Circulating out of Nigerian slang in the early 2010s, the resulting compound spread through Instagram and TikTok across Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Uganda, South Sudan, Zambia and South Africa. It describes a young woman, often accused of faking a lavish lifestyle online, said to rely on wealthy older men nicknamed "sponsors" to fund her designer clothes and vacations rather than earning them herself. For 10 points, give this two-word African slang term for a materialistic, status-obsessed woman.

An Urban Dictionary entry dated 18 April 2011 tied this two-word phrase to hippie subculture, but its viral second life began on Twitter on 24 March 2019, when music producer @umru_ used it while sizing up the atmosphere of an event he was organizing. Days later, on 2 April, another user's bare tweet of the phrase helped push it across the platform. That September, Tumblr user starion posted a comic of a man swinging a baseball bat while shouting it, spawning an absurdist genre of violent, blunt-object-wielding posts captioned with the same phrase. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase for informally assessing someone's mood or energy.

Written evidence for this term dates back to the 1950s, when people with physical disabilities used it to describe those without them, and Alcoholics Anonymous vocabulary later applied it to non-alcoholics. It appears in the 1987 film The Garbage Pail Kids Movie before crossing onto 4chan in the late 2000s, first showing up on the site's /r9k/ board in June 2012 and growing especially common within that board's greentext stories. Shortened from a word for "conventional" plus an informal diminutive suffix, it now functions online as a pejorative for someone whose tastes, fashion and hobbies are seen as unoriginal, mainstream and disconnected from internet subculture. For 10 points, give this dismissive slang term, often used by self-styled internet-savvy posters to describe an ordinary, mainstream person.

This company was founded in June 2012 by Dom Hofmann, Rus Yusupov and Colin Kroll, and was acquired by Twitter for a reported thirty million dollars before it had even launched. After launching on 24 January 2013, it grew to roughly forty million users within seven months on the strength of a looping six-second video format that seeded countless catchphrase memes covered elsewhere in this category, from a boy's wrong arithmetic answer to a girl's chicken misidentification. Citing weak monetization, high-profile creator departures and turmoil at its parent company, Twitter shut the service down on 18 January 2017. Hofmann later launched a spiritual successor app called Byte in January 2020, which itself shut down in 2023. For 10 points, name this defunct six-second video-looping app whose four-year run produced an outsized share of mid-2010s internet meme culture.

According to the humor site Cracked, this term originated in the late 1990s as a description for bad basketball players, having circulated earlier within African American Vernacular English and hip-hop culture. TLC's January 1999 hit single, the first release off their album FanMail, took its title from this same word, using it to deride men who lack their own car or place to live. Gaming culture gave the term an unrelated second life: in an October 2008 article, game designer David Sirlin defined it as describing players "handicapped by self-imposed rules that the game knows nothing about," tracing its gaming usage back to a Street Fighter II practice of repeatedly mashing buttons. For 10 points, give this slang term, alternately describing a broke, car-less man in a TLC song or a gamer hamstrung by imaginary house rules.

This word began as the past participle of a verb meaning "to illuminate" or "set aflame," and by 1914 had already picked up a slang sense of "drunk." Though that inebriated sense is over a century old, the term surged back into currency through African American Vernacular English and hip-hop culture, and by the 2010s its meaning had broadened from describing an intoxicated person to describing an exciting atmosphere, as in a party full of people in that older, alcohol-soaked sense. It exploded into mainstream slang between about 2013 and 2015, spreading largely through Vine, Twitter and Instagram. For 10 points, give this one-syllable slang adjective describing something extremely exciting or excellent.

The 15 September 2016 episode of a daytime talk show carried the ungainly title "I Want To Give Up My Car-Stealing, Knife-Wielding, Twerking 13-Year-Old Daughter Who Tried to Frame Me for a Crime." On that episode, after members of the studio audience laughed at her, the show's 13-year-old guest spun around and challenged them to a fight beyond the studio, delivering her confrontational ultimatum in a heavy, slang-inflected accent that internet commenters immediately began spelling out phonetically. An image macro built around her exact wording appeared online on 2 October 2016, and the girl behind it, Danielle Bregoli, parlayed her overnight infamy into a rap career under the stage name Bhad Bhabie, releasing a single sampling the clip on 24 January 2017 and signing a million-dollar recording contract soon after. For 10 points, give this phonetically spelled line yelled at a Dr. Phil studio audience by the girl who became Bhad Bhabie.
answer: cash me ousside, howbow dah [or catch me outside, how about that; or cash me outside how bout dat; prompt on partial answer]

question: This platform launched a free, safe-for-work streaming companion called OFTV in 2021, expanding beyond its main subscription business. Tim Stokely founded the London-based service in 2016 as a way for creators to monetize their content directly. Beyoncé mentioned it in her verse on the 2020 remix of Megan Thee Stallion’s song “Savage”. Its payment model includes monthly subscriptions, tips, and individual purchases of locked content, with creators receiving eighty percent of those fees. For 10 points, name this subscription platform where followers pay to access a creator’s exclusive photos and videos.

In the episode “One Krabs Trash”, a shopkeeper invokes this deceased character while inventing a curse to recover a valuable purchase. The trick backfires when the buyer actually locates this character’s grave and returns the supposedly cursed object to its occupant. That object is a soda-drinking cap which Mr. Krabs had sold before realizing how much money it might fetch. A large numeral on the front of the cap explains the boast associated with its former owner. For 10 points, name this SpongeBob SquarePants character celebrated by the exclamation “He was number one”.
answer: Smitty Werbenjägermanjensen [or Smitty Werbenjagermanjensen; or Smitty Werben Man Jensen; or Smitty Werben Jager Man Jensen; prompt on Smitty]

question: These comics are associated with Finnish artist Sakolut and the imageboard Kuvalauta, where early examples circulated in 2010. Their speech bubbles use deliberately mangled spelling alongside drawings that resemble hasty work in Microsoft Paint. Gooby, a distorted version of Goofy, appears alongside this character in the same chaotic cartoon universe. Other familiar animated figures, including Mickey Mouse and Bugs Bunny, receive similarly crude redesigns in related strips. For 10 points, name this misspelled internet parody of Disney’s sailor-suited Donald, the central character of these deliberately badly drawn webcomics.

A related lip-sync trend had each participant silently treating their companion as the less attractive member of the pair. The original clip attracted jokes about its speaker’s golden-looking eyes and his unusually unblinking delivery directly toward the camera. Uploaded to TikTok in October 2020 by jayrscottyy, the video shows its creator delivering an unsolicited opinion while sitting inside a car. His follow-up insists that one member of every close companionship must be ugly. For 10 points, give his opening catchphrase denying that a pair of inseparable companions can both be attractive.
answer: I ain’t never seen two pretty best friends [or I have never seen two pretty best friends; or two pretty best friends]

question: An early TikTok using this audio features cgleason22 debating whether to create a fake account to comment on his own videos. Another version applies the sound to Fiona concealing her nightly transformation into an ogre, turning the exchange into a Shrek joke. Participants lip-sync the dialogue while performing conspicuous acts of deception and pretending their behavior will escape detection. The exchange alternates between confident reassurance and an anxious objection that the deception will be discovered. For 10 points, give the reassuring catchphrase and skeptical follow-up question used in this viral audio about getting away with something.
answer: Nobody is gonna know. How would they know? [or Nobody’s gonna know; or Nobody is gonna know; or How would they know; or Nobody is going to know]

question: Jennifer Allen proposed this phenomenon’s clinical-sounding name in 2010 during an online discussion of an experience that lacked an agreed label. People describing it often report pleasant tingles beginning at the scalp and moving down the neck toward the upper spine. The same term also labels audiovisual media deliberately created to evoke that feeling in viewers or listeners. Common triggers include soft voices and small repetitive sounds, turning ordinary actions into material for an entire online video genre. For 10 points, give the four-letter abbreviation associated with relaxing videos of whispering and gentle tapping.

The image behind this meme comes from Wabbit Twouble, a 1941 cartoon in which its subject briefly imitates Elmer Fudd’s portly appearance. Reddit user GaryTheTaco paired the image with its familiar name in a mock PlayStation 4 game cover shared in 2018. Its spread included a GameStop manager’s story about a customer attempting to buy the nonexistent game pictured on that cover. Subsequent edits placed the same unusually round character into covers for other video games. For 10 points, name this meme depicting an enormous, chubby version of Bugs Bunny.

In a notorious fan animation, this line is delivered immediately before the visiting character flies away through a bedroom window. The scene ends with a declaration of devotion displayed over melancholy piano music, completing an unsettling parody of fandom. The surrounding internet phenomenon grew from a 2013 4chan story centered on obsessive admiration for a DreamWorks character. Its wording turns a familiar statement that something has finished into a pun based on the green visitor’s species. For 10 points, give this four-word Shrek meme catchphrase announcing that everything has come to an end.
answer: It’s all ogre now [or It is all ogre now]

question: A March 2019 reaction image imagined this animal sadly looking at a phone after its owner announced his engagement to Ryland Adams. Other posts turned the same engagement news into jokes about the animal’s imagined feelings toward the couple. The meme’s wider notoriety followed the resurfacing of a 2015 podcast story, which its owner said was a fabricated joke. He denied that the alleged incident had happened and posted apologies as the controversy spread online. For 10 points, identify this YouTuber’s pet at the center of the controversy, giving its owner and animal type.
answer: Shane Dawson’s cat [or Shane Dawson cat; or Shane Dawsons cat; prompt on Shane Dawson]

question: The advertisement opened by this phrase promoted a self-improvement program called “67 Steps to Wealth, Health, Love, and Happiness”. Its speaker claims to read a book daily and says mentors helped him escape a life with very little money. He points to shelves of books and insists that knowledge matters more to him than material possessions. Frequent appearances before YouTube videos in 2015 inspired numerous remixes of the pitch, delivered beside a Lamborghini. For 10 points, give the four-word opening catchphrase of Tai Lopez’s advertisement, identifying the place where he stores his car.

This character’s disastrous charge takes place in the Rookery of Upper Blackrock Spire, while the guild PalsForLife discusses its battle plan. Played by Ben Schulz, the character became famous through a video shared on a Warcraft fansite in May 2005. Blizzard later acknowledged the meme through an achievement, a trading card, and an appearance as a non-player character. In the clip, a paladin abruptly rushes into danger, abandoning the group’s careful preparations and leading the party to its destruction. For 10 points, name this World of Warcraft character who loudly shouts his own name as he charges.

A 2014 CollegeHumor sketch treats this label as a condition that a doctor can diagnose in a woman. In a 2012 viral video, lohanthony swings his leg while repeatedly calling out to people described by this term. Kreayshawn uses its plural form in “Gucci Gucci” when dismissing women who wear the designer brands named in the song. The insult characterizes someone’s personality or tastes as predictable, conformist, and lacking individuality, rather than sophisticated or distinctive. For 10 points, give this two-word slang insult for an unoriginal woman whose preferences seem entirely conventional.

This internet adjective is often paired with "bean" or with the deliberately misspelled opposite "lorge." Its early spread was linked to Twenty One Pilots fans, who used it for singer Tyler Joseph on Tumblr and Twitter. In June 2015, Joseph replied to the fandom by declaring that he was a bean. The word became a common hashtag for adorable animals, especially tiny birds, as well as fan art. For 10 points, give this deliberately misspelled adjective for something exceptionally tiny and cute.

This BetterTTV emote was submitted in February 2017 and depicts Pepe the Frog wearing a surprised expression. It developed as a frog-based counterpart to the older Twitch reaction image PogChamp. Stream viewers type this word to celebrate an exciting play or an unexpectedly impressive moment. Variants include Woggers and COGGERS, and its use outside streaming became a joke in its own right. For 10 points, name this Twitch expression of excitement ending in "-gers."

A related adjective for secondhand embarrassment was popularized by a character introduced in the British comic strip The Bash Street Kids in 1972. A Reddit community with this word in its name became a home for embarrassing and awkward videos. Online speakers use the word to react to a social blunder that produces secondhand embarrassment, discomfort, or pity. It has become a broad verdict on badly received posts, performances, and attempts at humor. For 10 points, give this one-word internet reaction for something painfully embarrassing to witness.

This slang verb began with the physical act of tightening a muscle, especially to display one’s arm. It later became a common rap and internet term for flaunting success, possessions, skill, or social status. Dictionary definitions now include both "to boast or brag" and "to show off" as informal senses. A person might do this with a luxury car, expensive clothes, or a conspicuous achievement. For 10 points, give this short slang verb for showing off.

This compliment is frequently paired with "ate," a slang verb praising an outstanding performance, outfit, or argument. It imagines a plate cleaned so completely that no trace remains, extending a food metaphor into praise. Social-media users apply it after someone performs flawlessly or dominates an exchange. The phrase became broadly popular online around 2017 and 2018, without a single attributable creator. For 10 points, give this three-word praise meaning that someone did something perfectly, leaving nothing to criticize.
answer: left no crumbs [or left no crumb; or no crumbs left]

question: This phrase appeared in hip-hop songs by Young Scooter and Lil B in 2012 before becoming widespread in memes. A 2017 tweet by rapper Kash Doll helped establish its modern use for someone desperate for romantic or intimate attention. Internet users create exaggerated variants by replacing its second word with "atrocious," "terrible," or "horrendous." It can also describe general hardship or despair outside its common relationship context. For 10 points, give this two-word slang phrase for being desperately thirsty for affection.

This form of manipulation takes its name from Patrick Hamilton’s 1938 thriller play about a husband who tries to make his wife doubt her sanity. In the story, he repeatedly denies that the household lamps flicker even though they do. The term entered much wider online political discourse after a 2016 Teen Vogue article about false claims and reversals. It also became one part of a three-word 2021 parody of the phrase "Live, Laugh, Love." In internet slang, it means deliberately supplying false information to make a person question memory, perception, or reality. For 10 points, name this manipulative practice.

In Black drag culture, the letter T came to mean truth or revealing personal information, and the sound-alike beverage later became the familiar spelling. This phrase asks a speaker to share gossip, secrets, or the real story behind a situation. It spread well beyond its original communities through social media and is a common feature of get-ready-with-me videos. A listener uses it when inviting a friend to reveal what happened. For 10 points, give this three-word request for gossip.
answer: spill the tea [or spill tea; or spill the T]

question: A classic joke illustrating this practice challenges a supposed music fan to name three albums by a band they claim to enjoy. It occurs when a community restricts access to information or treats newcomers as illegitimate members. A subreddit created in 2016 collects examples of that behavior. Online discussion of the practice surged after an ironic three-word 2021 parody of "Live, Laugh, Love." For 10 points, give this term for policing who belongs in a fandom or may share an interest.

This verb developed from the title of a 2000 Eminem song on The Marshall Mathers LP, featuring vocals by Dido. That song tells the story of an obsessive fan who writes increasingly alarming letters to the rapper. By 2017, the Oxford English Dictionary had added the resulting term for an excessively enthusiastic fan. Online fandoms often use "we" followed by this verb to express admiration for a singer, athlete, company, or fictional character. For 10 points, give this four-letter verb meaning to be an intensely devoted fan.

This phrase grew from the competitive "reading" tradition of New York drag ballroom culture. In the 1990 documentary Paris Is Burning, performer Dorian Corey distinguishes it from a direct insult. Voguing dancers also used movement to direct this kind of contempt toward rivals. Modern dictionaries define the expression as an indirect, artful public criticism. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase for making a subtle, disdainful insult.

This insult appeared in rap lyrics long before its large TikTok revival, including a 1992 Sir Mix-a-Lot song. Its modern online use often targets someone who offers excessive devotion to a person they are attracted to without reciprocal interest. It can overlap with terms such as "white knight" and "orbiter." A TikTok trend grouped such admirers into a fictitious nation after describing their behavior. For 10 points, give this four-letter term for an excessively submissive admirer.

This catchphrase often follows the setup "I have one question for you" before a camera points toward an unfashionable item. It became a major Vine catchphrase in the middle of the 2010s. Its best-known early clip has a teenager confront a police officer about his footwear. The joke later broadened to mock any odd clothing choice or object. For 10 points, give this shouted four-word question used to ridicule someone’s shoes.

Sophia Amoruso popularized this term with her 2014 memoir about building Nasty Gal. A Netflix series bearing the same title helped spread it further in 2017. The word originally celebrated women’s ambition and entrepreneurial success, but it later acquired an ironic edge. Critics use it to question a version of empowerment tied to overwork, capitalism, and corporate ambition. For 10 points, name this label for a career-focused woman, often now used ironically.

This phrase describes a person so immersed in internet culture that their vocabulary, references, and sense of proportion become detached from offline life. It is often used critically or self-mockingly when someone treats a niche platform dispute as overwhelmingly important. Near-synonyms replace its first modifier with "terminally" or "extremely." The term became widespread as social-media discourse increasingly supplied everyday language and cultural reference points. For 10 points, give this two-word label for someone excessively immersed in the internet.

This word once referred literally to a blow or force, then developed an American slang sense of political influence in the nineteenth century. Internet users now apply it to the social power, attention, and credibility a person has within a community. Rappers helped make the word fashionable in its current cultural sense. Someone who chases it may post provocatively in hopes of gaining followers or visibility. For 10 points, give this five-letter slang term for social influence and status.

The base adjective in this phrase became prominent in competitive gaming communities as an insult for an opponent bitter about a loss. Its American slang sense of angry or irritated dates to 1938. Fighting-game and multiplayer communities helped carry it across the internet, and a series of Smash Bros. videos highlighted losing players with it in the title. The added abbreviation intensifies the expression. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase for being extremely bitter or resentful.

This contraction is a feature of African American English and Southern speech. It developed from "fixing to" and signals that an action is imminent or intended. It is commonly used before another verb, much like "about to" or "going to." A 2025 meme deliberately mangled it alongside other queer and AAVE slang to parody people who imitate expressions without understanding them. For 10 points, give this five-letter contraction meaning "about to."

In journalism, this term describes deliberately provocative commentary rushed out in response to a news event with little reporting or reflection. Online, users often announce one before offering an unpopular opinion about a film, game, celebrity, or cultural issue. The phrase can be earnest, but it is also frequently used sarcastically to mock an obvious or poorly considered claim. It combines a temperature adjective with a noun for an opinion. For 10 points, give this two-word label for a provocative, quickly stated opinion.

This phrase comes from a Tim & Eric Awesome Show, Great Job! sketch in which a house is offered to Jim Boonie. The sketch appeared in the March 2009 episode "Presidents" and parodies a commercial offering a house at no cost to one man. At its end, Tim Heidecker whispers this line directly to the camera. It later became a popular GIF and bait-and-switch punchline on YouTube. For 10 points, give this four-word Tim and Eric catchphrase about a no-cost property.
answer: It’s free real estate [or It is free real estate; or free real estate]

question: This joke phrase turns a conventional condolence into a pizza topping. It is often used online after a fictional character, a joke, or an old meme has met an ignominious end. The phrase plays on a familiar three-letter condolence abbreviation and an expression of mourning. Image macros sometimes present it as a deliberately absurd variation on a standard condolence. For 10 points, give this humorous three-word eulogy involving a cured meat.
answer: rest in pepperonis [or RIP in pepperonis; or rest in pepperoni]

question: This 2021 catchphrase combines a shortened term for suspiciousness from Among Us with a Japanese word meaning "fool." TikToker Akeam Francis made videos containing variations of the phrase, which then supplied sounds for edits across social media. An early related clip shows Francis yelling at a character named Deku. The expression became a deliberately childish way to accuse someone of suspicious behavior. For 10 points, give this two-word internet phrase combining gaming slang and Japanese.

In Among Us, impostors can use these passages to travel secretly between rooms, whereas crewmates cannot. Spotting a player emerge from one often supplies evidence in a discussion and can lead to an ejection. A widely used image template shows a red crewmate inside one of these openings. The action became central to the game’s slang about suspicious players. For 10 points, name this hidden passage used by impostors for rapid movement.

This retort comes from a SpongeBob SquarePants scene in which a pink starfish answers the telephone at the Krusty Krab. A caller asks whether they have reached that restaurant, and the confused employee treats the question as an inquiry about his identity. The exchange ends when the caller angrily hangs up. Online, the line became a reaction to an annoying question or a case of obvious misunderstanding. For 10 points, give this four-word SpongeBob response, usually punctuated with a comma after its first word.
answer: No, This Is Patrick [or No This Is Patrick]

question: This reaction image shows a normally grumpy SpongeBob SquarePants character after his face has been dramatically reshaped into a conventionally attractive one. The underlying scene occurs in an episode after a flying doorknob repeatedly strikes him. A short loop of his pleased expression is also used online under an alternate title describing a tumble. Captions use the altered face to signal an unexpectedly polished or attractive result. For 10 points, name this meme, whose title begins with an adjective for good-looking.

This rallying cry originated with Caesar’s signed message in a 2011 film about a primate uprising. Its longer form contrasts the weakness of an individual primate with collective power. Reddit users had adopted primate imagery for themselves by the 2021 GameStop short squeeze, helping turn the line into an investing-community slogan. It now broadly signals solidarity among a group facing a more powerful opponent. For 10 points, give this three-word phrase associated with retail-investor memes.
answer: Apes Together Strong [or Ape Together Strong; or Apes Strong Together]

question: This WallStreetBets expression praises someone who refuses to sell a position during a sharp decline or volatile trading period. It is frequently represented by a gem emoji followed by raised-palms emoji. The term became especially visible during the 2021 GameStop short squeeze, while its opposite describes investors who sell too early. It later spread through cryptocurrency communities as well. For 10 points, give this two-word slang term for unwaveringly holding an investment.

This ironic declaration precedes an absurdly reckless or clever action in clips and captioned images. It originated in a 2019 Vsauce video titled "LET'S PLAY SUPER MARIO QUADRATICS," where Michael Stevens says it before selecting a menu option. The quotation was repurposed online to frame ordinary bad decisions as expert-level tactics. For 10 points, give this three-word label for that supposed expert tactic.
answer: Pro Gamer Move [or I’m Gonna Do What’s Called a Pro Gamer Move; or I'm Gonna Do What's Called a Pro Gamer Move]

question: This ironic reaction label is applied to an especially impressive, lucky, or memorable event during play. It developed in the late 2010s alongside a related euphemism for a controversial lapse during play. Users also deploy it sarcastically when a clip’s result is embarrassing, trivial, or far less impressive than the praise suggests. The wording combines an adjective of grand praise with a reference to players and a brief event. For 10 points, give this three-word online reaction phrase.

This term names a dangerous form of online harassment that seeks to provoke an emergency-police response at a target’s address through a false report. It became closely associated with gaming feuds and livestreamers, though it can target anyone. The name alludes to a specialized police unit often expected to respond. A 2017 hoax call following a gaming dispute in Wichita resulted in the death of an uninvolved resident. For 10 points, give this term for the criminal hoax.

This unfair gaming practice involves watching an opponent’s live broadcast to obtain information that the game itself has not provided. A viewer may use the feed to learn a player’s location, strategy, or private lobby details before joining the same match. Competition rules often prohibit it, sometimes calling it "ghosting." Broadcaster privacy modes can conceal identifying details in an effort to reduce the practice. For 10 points, name this conduct that exploits a live broadcast during a game.

This four-letter post-match abbreviation combines a conventional compliment with a taunt that claims the contest required little effort. Players commonly type it into all-chat after winning, so opponents often read it as poor sportsmanship. In Overwatch, a chat filter famously replaced the phrase with self-deprecating canned messages. For 10 points, give this gaming-chat shorthand for "good game, easy."

This social-media prompt asks viewers to look at a person’s clothes. Here, its first word is a shortened name for a clothing ensemble, rather than a reference to physical size. A post with this label typically features a photograph or short video showing off a styled look, often with the hashtag of the same name. The expression has appeared on social media since at least 2017. For 10 points, give this two-word request to assess someone’s attire.

This Internet insult labels a person as passive, weak, or submissive in contrast to a supposedly dominant "alpha." It derives from animal-hierarchy terminology whose popular application to humans rests on an oversimplified and discredited model. The label circulated especially in manosphere forums before spreading into broader online discourse, often ironically. For 10 points, give this Greek-letter term when used as that pejorative label.

This brightly clad character was one of the recurring figures in George Miller’s absurdist YouTube comedy universe. Wearing a lycra bodysuit, he helped launch the 2013 Harlem Shake dance trend in a video by Miller’s Filthy Frank channel. The character also released a comedy-rap album in 2017, before Miller’s later music career as Joji. For 10 points, name this Filthy Frank character whose name combines a color with a generic term for a man.

This annual video series summarized major creators, music, and trends on its platform from the preceding year. It began in 2010 and ran through 2019. Its 2018 installment surpassed Justin Bieber’s "Baby" to become the platform’s most-disliked video while public dislike counts were visible. The following year’s entry switched to a comparatively simple list format after the backlash. For 10 points, name this discontinued annual video recap series.

This cult YouTube compilation was created by user eljolto on December 30, 2015. It assembled more than 300 very short clips, many of which became memes in their own right. The collection accumulated hundreds of millions of views and appeared widely in recommendation sidebars before its removal. Its entries included the "Yee" dinosaur clip, "He-Man Sings," and "Have You Ever Had a Dream Like This?" For 10 points, name this compilation whose two-word title grandly asserts the value of its contents.

This deliberately childish catchphrase is used online to dismiss a subject as too silly to deserve a serious response. It began with a December 2016 Twitter parody of a poster for The Bye Bye Man, which renamed the horror character. The phrase later gained fresh exposure after PewDiePie used it in a Minecraft Let’s Play. It can appear as an ironic caption or as a lowbrow way to belittle a discussion. For 10 points, give this four-part internet catchphrase formed from two repeated nursery-style words.

This question is asked when an image appears to hide the layout of a famous four-panel webcomic. That source strip, published by Tim Buckley in Ctrl+Alt+Del on June 2, 2008, made an abrupt turn from the comic’s usual gaming humor to a serious hospital scene. Online parodies reduce its character positions to a pattern often rendered as one vertical line, then two figures, then two figures, then a vertical and horizontal line. For 10 points, give this five-word meme-recognition question.
answer: Is This Loss? [or is this loss; prompt on Loss; accept Loss.jpg]

question: This performer's name became such a global search-engine phenomenon that it's still used online as shorthand for instant, meme-level fame, despite an on-camera career that lasted barely three months. Born in Beirut in 1993, she was raised in a conservative Catholic household before her family relocated to the United States around 2000. She debuted in adult film in October 2014, and within two months had been named the number-one ranked performer on a major streaming platform. A single scene in which she wore a hijab triggered a wave of death threats and international backlash, despite her having left Lebanon as a child. She exited the industry in early 2015 having reportedly earned about $12,000 total from roughly a dozen scenes, later reinventing herself as a webcam model, sports-talk podcast host, and OnlyFans creator. For 10 points, name this Lebanese-American figure whose brief career made her one of the internet's most-searched names of the 2010s.

Born in Loxahatchee, Florida in 1991, she studied psychology at Florida State University for a single semester, hoping to become a teacher, before leaving school in 2010 to enter the adult film industry at age nineteen. She won NightMoves' Best New Starlet award in 2012 and XBIZ's equivalent the following year, then took home the XBIZ Female Performer of the Year award in 2014 and the AVN equivalent in 2016. She was inducted into the XRCO Hall of Fame in 2021 and the AVN Hall of Fame in 2025. More recently she has ranked among OnlyFans' top earners, struck a content partnership with Playboy Plus, and co-founded the AI-creator platform Clona. For 10 points, name this performer, one of the adult industry's most decorated stars of the 2010s.

This originally gender-neutral Japanese term, whose two characters mean "two" and "form," is traced by some etymologists to depictions of dual-sexed figures in the Heian- and Kamakura-era hand scroll Yamai no Sōshi, or "Scroll of Afflictions." Historically the word could describe any real or fictional person seen as possessing both masculine and feminine physical traits, but usage narrowed sharply in the 1990s as it came to denote a specific character archetype and genre within erotic Japanese comics and animation, or hentai. Today the term most often labels drawn characters combining male and female anatomical features, and by extension the pornographic genre built around them. For 10 points, give this Japanese loanword, often clipped to its first syllable, for this hentai subgenre.

Filmed reactions to this video predate the modern YouTube reaction-channel format by years, with celebrities including Joe Rogan and Kobe Bryant among those recorded watching it during its 2007-2008 viral peak. Its spread relied on a dare format, where a person would challenge a friend to watch it unprepared and film the resulting horror, creating a secondary viral loop distinct from the original clip. Only about a minute long, it surfaced on English-language shock sites in mid-2007 after originating overseas, and it later inspired a parody segment on South Park in which the show's fourth-graders are shown reacting to it. For 10 points, name this notorious scatological video, whose four-word title counts its performers and names the vessel they share.

This February 2013 video trend uses a short excerpt from a trap track by Baauer. A typical version opens with one person dancing while nearby people remain still; after the beat drops, a cut reveals the entire group performing wildly in costumes. The format inspired thousands of uploads per day at its peak and helped prompt Billboard to incorporate YouTube views into the Hot 100. The song then debuted at number one under the revised chart rules. For 10 points, name this viral dance-video meme and song title.

This name was first applied on 4chan’s /r9k/ board to original illustrations and photoshops of a green cartoon frog, presented as scarce trading cards. Some early images included watermarks that jokingly preserved their supposed value. In 2016, the concept developed into a blockchain collectible project whose cards could be traded through Counterparty. Its directory ultimately catalogued 1,774 official cards across 36 series. For 10 points, give this two-word name for those collectible frog-image cards.

This online behavior involves deliberately posting provocative, insincere, or off-topic remarks to draw an emotional response and derail a discussion. Its name evokes a fishing method that drags bait through water to see what will bite. The online sense emerged in the late 1980s or early 1990s in Usenet discussion groups, including a baiting phrase directed at newcomers. For 10 points, name this baiting practice in online discussions.

This blue, sneaker-wearing shark is widely regarded as the first character in the Italian brainrot trend. An early AI-generated version circulated on TikTok in January 2025, accompanied by an exaggerated pseudo-Italian voiceover. Its visual design gives the shark three elongated fin-legs, each with a blue Nike shoe. The character’s nonsense, rhyming name became a repeatable catchphrase across short-form video. For 10 points, name this shark character of Italian brainrot.

This Italian-brainrot creature combines the head of a large reptile with the body and wings of a military aircraft. Its AI-generated images and rhyming text-to-speech narration began circulating on TikTok in February 2025. The earliest located post was uploaded by @armenjiharhanyan on February 20. It became one of the best-known absurd animal-object hybrids in the trend alongside a sneaker-wearing shark. For 10 points, name this reptile-aircraft hybrid.

This portmanteau blends slang for enduring a loss with the name of an addictive narcotic to describe a fictional inhaled substance. A prominent reaction image depicts Pepe the Frog connected to a tank bearing this label. The word appeared on 4chan’s /int/ board in 2018, and a tank image appeared on /pol/ the following year. It later became a widely used Twitch-chat emote for mocking excuses or denial. For 10 points, name this internet slang term.

On 4chan, this act is an attempt to make a post whose numerical ID ends in two identical digits. An ID ending in three, four, or more matching digits is instead called a trip, quad, or higher repetition. Users treat posting at the desired number as a matter of chance, sometimes making a thread outcome conditional on success. The practice appears in threads whose posters urge others to "check" their digits. For 10 points, name this practice, usually spelled with a final "s" or "z."
answer: rolling dubs [or rolling dubz; or roll dubs; or roll dubz]

question: This Minecraft creator became known for appearing behind a round white mask with a simple smiley face. His invite-only multiplayer server, launched in April 2020 with GeorgeNotFound, featured improvised storylines among a group of creators. In October 2022, he revealed his face in a video titled "hi, I’m ___." The video trended widely, and he later removed it after hostile reactions to his appearance. For 10 points, name this YouTuber, whose channel has drawn tens of millions of subscribers.

This made-up condition is introduced in a bait-and-switch joke by asking what it is, then delivering a crude sound-alike punchline. It went viral in July 2018 through a false Instagram rumor that Fortnite streamer Ninja had died from it. The hoax prompted widespread mock memorial posts, confusion among fans, and follow-up jokes by PewDiePie and other creators. For 10 points, name this fictional illness with a five-letter name.

This two-word prank phrase became a major viral joke after WelvenDaGreat posted a March 2015 Instagram clip in which he claimed that it had arrived in the mail. The setup invites a listener to ask a question that enables a crude phonetic punchline, often followed by "got ’em." A teenage independent candidate who adopted the phrase as a pseudonym briefly appeared in polls during the 2016 U.S. presidential race. For 10 points, give this bait-and-switch expression.

This SpongeBob SquarePants line is repeatedly asked of the show’s restaurant owner during an attempt to restore his youthful spirit. The scene comes from the season-three episode "Mid-Life Crustacean," in which SpongeBob and Patrick take him out for a night on the town. Online edits often distort the footage or replace its audio to turn the question into a surreal reaction. For 10 points, give this seven-word question addressed to the show’s penny-pinching character.
answer: Are You Feeling It Now, Mr. Krabs? [or Are You Feeling It Now Mr Krabs; or Are You Feeling It Yet, Mr. Krabs?]

question: This fictional address is written on a diver’s mask in Finding Nemo. Dory repeatedly recites it in order to help Marlin find the dentist who has taken Nemo. The phrase became a memorable online quotation because of Dory’s forgetfulness and her eventual recollection of the clue. It starts with the dentist’s initial and surname, followed by a street number, a street name, and the Australian city. For 10 points, give this address from Finding Nemo.
answer: P. Sherman, 42 Wallaby Way, Sydney [or P Sherman 42 Wallaby Way Sydney; or 42 Wallaby Way, Sydney]

question: This two-word sound bite came from MaxMoeFoe’s May 2016 video "Edward Watermelon-Hands." In the scene, Ian Carter jumps down from a table, delivers the line, and laughs alongside MaxMoeFoe and Filthy Frank. Edits then paired the audio with clips of people or characters falling, helping it spread through YouTube and Vine remixes. For 10 points, give this self-identifying line from that online meme.

This two-word sound bite consists of an imperative followed by a racial slur. It circulated as an intentionally confrontational quote from creator Ian Carter's early shock-comedy-era videos and became a recurring reference in fan edits. The phrase is often invoked by name when discussing the controversial language that characterized his older content. For 10 points, give this quote; accept the uncensored wording.

This approval reaction comes from Will Smith’s appearance in YouTube Rewind 2018. While looking through a pair of large binoculars at the Fortnite Battle Bus, Smith laughs and says this line twice. Editors soon used the binocular view as an exploitable template, inserting anything Smith was supposedly admiring. The scene became one of the few enduring meme formats from the heavily criticized recap video. For 10 points, give this three-word Will Smith quote about what he sees through binoculars.
answer: Ah, that’s hot [or Ah, that's hot; or that’s hot; or that's hot]

question: This abrupt, resonant clang became a random punchline in ironic video edits on YouTube, TikTok, and iFunny. Its original audio file has a long, underscore-separated name mentioning a pole. YouTuber Jixaw first used it in a September 2020 follower-special video, and later uploaded the isolated audio. One-hour versions, loud remixes, and streamer audio libraries helped spread it further. For 10 points, name this meme audio produced when a long object clatters to the ground.
answer: falling metal pipe [or metal pipe falling sound effect; or metal pipe falling; or metal pipe sound effect]

question: This 2021 TikTok trend asked students to post videos showing stolen or damaged school property as a boast. Its name uses slang for a successful theft and a modifier meaning sneaky or malicious. Reports from schools around the United States led to discipline, arrests, and a platform effort to remove associated videos and redirect related hashtags. A countertrend called "angelic yields" encouraged students to leave supplies or gifts instead. For 10 points, name this school-harm TikTok challenge.

This accusation means that screenshots or recordings provide clear evidence of someone doing something embarrassing, dishonest, or socially frowned upon. Its wording invokes ultra-high-definition video resolution, exaggerating how undeniable the proof is. The expression entered wide meme use after a 2019 RDCworld1 sketch about lawyers defending rappers, then spread as a reaction on social media. For 10 points, give this phrase for being exposed by apparently unmistakable evidence.

This one-syllable slang adjective dismisses a song, film, outfit, game, or opinion as merely average or underwhelming. It developed from an older music and cannabis sense for low-to-medium quality before becoming a widespread online put-down in the early 2020s. A person using it is not necessarily calling something terrible; they are saying it failed to be impressive. For 10 points, give this common online judgment meaning mediocre.

This product was advertised by spokesman Phil Swift, who demonstrates its extreme adhesion by repairing a leaking water tank. A 2017 review by JonTron helped make the commercial a meme, and later image macros show Swift using the product to solve absurdly large problems. Its name combines a quality of bending with a generic adhesive strip. For 10 points, name this heavily advertised waterproof adhesive product.

This snowclone names an exceptionally persuasive character trait by giving it the maximum value on a role-playing-game-style skill tree. It derives from image macros based on Skyrim's constellation-like perk menus and is often captioned beneath someone who has made an unusually convincing argument. Variants substitute traits such as sneak or wholesomeness. For 10 points, give this meme phrase for maximum persuasive ability.

This profane reaction is shouted after a disc golfer sends a throw wildly across a road instead of toward the basket. The seven-second clip became a reaction meme for a baffling mistake or a move that makes a situation worse. Sanitized variants replace its expletive with milder swear words. For 10 points, give this exasperated question directed at the thrower.
answer: What the fuck, Richard? [or What the fuck Richard; or What the heck, Richard?; or WTF Richard]

question: This electronic-music video depicts red crustaceans dancing on an island, while its 2018 release by Noisestorm coincided with Monstercat's April Fools' Day. Editors use its upbeat house track and animated creatures in remixes, celebrations, and captions that replace the original words. For 10 points, name this upbeat dance-music meme.

This caption accompanies General Grievous holding a newly acquired lightsaber in Revenge of the Sith. It became a reaction image to celebrate acquiring a desired object to a growing stash, particularly after a purchase or a successful acquisition. Its speaker is the Separatist leader known for displaying weapons taken from Jedi. For 10 points, give this Grievous quotation uttered after acquiring a new weapon.
answer: Another Fine Addition to My Collection [or another fine addition]

question: This reaction image shows android detective Yutaro Katori pointing at a butterfly and confidently misidentifying it. The still comes from the 1991 anime The Brave Fighter of Sun Fighbird and gained renewed popularity through Tumblr and other platforms in 2018. It is used when someone mistakes one thing for a superficially similar but clearly different one. For 10 points, give the question Katori asks in this meme.
answer: Is This a Pigeon? [or is this a pigeon]

question: This reaction image shows a man in a suit giving a puzzled, hurt expression. The frame is from the South African television series Generations: The Legacy and spread from South African Twitter to Reddit in 2018. It is captioned to convey the feeling that someone or something has been disrespected, ignored, or treated absurdly. For 10 points, give this rhetorical question used by that meme.
answer: Am I a Joke to You? [or am I a joke to you]

question: This image macro uses a still of Dave Chappelle in a suit, raising a finger during a parody campaign advertisement. The still originated in the 2004 Chappelle's Show sketch about healthcare and became a widespread reaction format on Reddit in late 2018. It frames an unconventional, sometimes absurd workaround as brilliant thinking. For 10 points, give this caption about contemporary difficulties and their answers.
answer: Modern Problems Require Modern Solutions [or modern problem requires modern solution]

question: This sarcastic reaction image comes from an El País video in which chess commentator Leontxo García reenacts a 1940 game between Ludwig Rellstab and Efim Bogoljubow. While shifting pieces on a magnetic board, García praises a play in Spanish, and a screenshot became an image macro. Online users apply the English caption to a plan that is clever, disastrous, or both. For 10 points, give this two-word chess-meme commendation.

This reaction phrase accompanies a screenshot of Thanos in Avengers: Infinity War defending a painful sacrifice. The image macro is used to dryly justify giving up something minor or major for a desired outcome. It became a common response format after the 2018 film's release and is distinct from the villain's quotation about balance. For 10 points, give this Thanos line about the cost of redemption.
answer: A Small Price to Pay for Salvation [or It's a Small Price to Pay for Salvation]

question: This Thanos quotation from Avengers: Infinity War became an online response to evenly matched quantities, equal vote totals, or a satisfying distribution. It is frequently paired with images of the villain, particularly in jokes about preserving an exact numerical equilibrium. Its speaker is the Marvel antagonist seeking to halve the universe's population. For 10 points, give this statement praising an ideal state of equilibrium.
answer: Perfectly Balanced, as All Things Should Be [or Perfect Balance, as All Things Should Be; or perfectly balanced]

question: This image macro comes from a December 2019 fundraising video for Bernie Sanders's presidential campaign. Wearing a winter coat outdoors, Sanders makes a direct appeal before a federal filing deadline; editors replaced the final object of his request with mundane or absurd demands. The still became a widely used template in early 2020. For 10 points, give the opening words of Sanders's repeated appeal.
answer: I Am Once Again Asking [or I Am Once Again Asking for Your Financial Support; or once again asking]

question: This slang insult literally denotes someone who uses a smokable form of cocaine, but online it is often used hyperbolically for a person acting erratically, impulsively, or with extreme frantic energy. Because that usage can stigmatize addiction, it is best understood as a rude meme label rather than a clinical description. For 10 points, give this compound word formed from a drug nickname and a word for a person.

This meme features former child actor Brett Ambler enthusiastically teaching other children to play a small buzzing instrument. The footage comes from the 1989 children's program Special Friends; a 2011 YouTube upload and a widely shared 2014 edit turned it into a remix source. A reaction clip from the footage questions another child’s identity. For 10 points, name this child-character meme.
answer: Kazoo Kid [or You on Kazoo; or Wait a Minute, Who Are You?]

question: This phrase sarcastically labels a trivial inconvenience that is possible only because someone has relative wealth, comfort, or access to modern conveniences. A common image macro pairs such a complaint with a crying woman touching her temple, while other versions use a slumped teenager. It became a popular internet tag and meme in the late 2000s and early 2010s. For 10 points, give this expression for a privileged minor complaint.
answer: First World Problems [or First World Problem; or 1st World Problems]

question: This dismissive catchphrase came from a 2012 local-news interview with Kimberly "Sweet Brown" Wilkins after she escaped an apartment fire. Her remarks about smoke inhalation were remixed into a Gregory Brothers song about bronchitis, helping the line spread widely. It is now used to reject a task, delay, or annoyance as undeserving of attention. For 10 points, give the line she used to dismiss her troubles.
answer: Ain't Nobody Got Time for That [or ain’t nobody got time for that; or nobody got time for that]

question: This line was repeatedly said by Joshua Holz while filming Snapchat clips of his classmate Daniel Lara and his outfits. The 2016 compilation, commonly called Damn Daniel, became viral on Twitter and made the featured shoe brand a central joke; Lara later received a lifetime supply from that company on Ellen. For 10 points, give this observation about Daniel's recurring footwear.
answer: Back at It Again with the White Vans [or back at it again with them white Vans; or white Vans]

question: This postscript is paired with an image of Kermit the Frog sipping a glass of tea. Beginning on Instagram in 2014, the format lets a user make a sarcastic criticism of another person's behavior and then pretend to withdraw from the matter. It is also known as Kermit Sipping Tea or Kermit Drinking Tea. For 10 points, give this ironic disclaimer about not being involved.
answer: But That's None of My Business [or but that’s none of my business; or none of my business]

question: This broad label describes an image or video joke that is deliberately rough, poorly compressed, pixelated, or minimally edited. Its visual flaws can signal irony, speed, or an anti-polished aesthetic, and it is sometimes used by moderators as a catchall for minimally crafted posts. Unlike a particular character or quotation, it names a general level of production value. For 10 points, give this three-word term for intentionally rough and poorly produced internet humor.

This visual style runs an image through many filters and repeated compression until it becomes grainy, oversaturated, discolored, and often difficult to read. The earliest known use of its food-metaphor name appeared on Tumblr in 2015, and dedicated Reddit communities helped popularize the style. A secondary nickname compares its distortion to an image subjected to an explosion. For 10 points, name this heavily distorted image-macro style.
answer: Deep Fried Meme [or Deep Fried Memes; or deep-fried meme; or nuked meme]

question: This internet term describes audio intentionally made extremely loud, clipped, and distorted in order to startle or overwhelm listeners. It originated on YTMND in 2005 and later became common in YouTube Poops, screamers, montage parodies, and abrupt video-edit punchlines. The phrase uses an assault metaphor and is often written as one word. For 10 points, name this harsh online-audio style.

This reaction image shows Doge striking Cheems with a stick, accompanied by an onomatopoeic impact sound. It originated in a March 2020 iFunny post and spread as a reply to overtly sexual posts or thirst-posting on social media. Edits replace the dogs or add characters from other franchises. For 10 points, give this meme command that sends the recipient to a fictional prison.
answer: Bonk, Go to Horny Jail [or Go to Horny Jail; or bonk]

question: This polite but absurd reaction catchphrase comes from a 2017 deep-fried image macro featuring Shaquille O'Neal at a drive-through. In the original setup, he requests food, is told the food is broken, and accepts the refusal before flashing a peace sign.
